title: How a fired 24-year-old built a $30 billion defense company
sentences: Palmer Luckey was born in California in 1992 and was homeschooled.
As a teenager he repaired broken phones and built virtual reality headsets in his parents' garage.
In 2012 his Oculus Rift Kickstarter asked for 250,000 dollars and raised about 2.4 million.
Two years later, Facebook bought Oculus for around two billion dollars.
Then in 2016, a 10,000 dollar political donation turned Silicon Valley against him.
By 2017 he was out of Facebook, at just 24 years old.
That same year he founded Anduril, building autonomous drones and defense software.
By 2025, Anduril was valued at more than 30 billion dollars.
Was getting fired the best thing that ever happened to him?

title: Why Nvidia was started in a Denny's booth
sentences: In 1993, three engineers sat in a Denny's restaurant in San Jose and planned a chip company.
One of them, Jensen Huang, had once washed dishes and waited tables at Denny's.
Their company, Nvidia, bet that computers would need special chips for graphics.
Its first product flopped, and by 1996 Nvidia was weeks away from running out of money.
Huang cut more than half the staff and bet everything on one new chip, the RIVA 128.
It worked, and Nvidia survived.
Decades later, those same graphics chips turned out to be perfect for training AI.
In 2025 Nvidia became the first company worth four trillion dollars.
Where is the next trillion-dollar idea being sketched tonight?

title: How cereal boxes saved Airbnb
sentences: In 2008, two designers in San Francisco could not pay their rent.
So they put air mattresses on their floor and rented them to strangers.
That became Airbnb, but almost nobody wanted to invest.
Deep in credit card debt, the founders tried something strange.
During the 2008 election they sold cereal boxes called Obama O's and Cap'n McCain's.
They raised about 30,000 dollars, enough to keep the company alive.
That stunt helped get them into the startup program Y Combinator.
Today Airbnb has hosted well over a billion guest arrivals.
What crazy side hustle would you try to save your dream?

title: Why Apple fired Steve Jobs and then begged him back
sentences: In 1985, Steve Jobs was forced out of Apple, the company he had co-founded.
He was 30 years old and called it devastating.
He started a new computer company called NeXT and bought a small studio that became Pixar.
Meanwhile Apple was losing money and, by 1997, was close to collapse.
So Apple bought NeXT for about 400 million dollars, and Jobs came back.
NeXT's software became the base of macOS and later the iPhone.
Within ten years, Apple went from near bankruptcy to changing the world with one phone.
Can losing everything be the start of something bigger?

title: Why SpaceX almost died on its fourth launch
sentences: SpaceX's first rocket, Falcon 1, failed in 2006.
It failed again in 2007, and a third time in August 2008.
Elon Musk later said the company only had money for about four attempts.
Tesla was also running out of cash in the middle of a financial crisis.
On September 28, 2008, the fourth Falcon 1 lifted off.
It reached orbit, the first privately developed liquid-fuel rocket to do it.
Months later, NASA gave SpaceX a 1.6 billion dollar cargo contract.
Today SpaceX launches more rockets than any other organization on Earth.
Would you have bet everything on attempt number four?

title: Why James Dyson built 5,127 failed vacuums
sentences: In the late 1970s, James Dyson got angry at his vacuum cleaner.
It kept losing suction because its bag clogged with dust.
He wondered if a spinning cyclone could pull dust out of the air instead.
Over about five years he built 5,127 prototypes, and every one but the last fell short.
He went deep into debt, and big companies refused to license his idea.
So he launched it himself in 1993, under his own name.
The bagless Dyson became one of Britain's best selling vacuums.
Could you keep going after five thousand failures?
